questions.q: A client says 'we need AI for invoices'. In the FDE loop, what should you do before building anything?
options: Pick the best model and start a proof of concept
Watch the clerks do the real work and collect real examples
Send the client a slide deck of AI use cases
Ask the finance director to write the requirements
questions.why: Discover comes before Frame and Build, because the request is not yet a problem you can solve.

questions.q: Which of these is a framed problem in the sense of the FDE loop?
options: Use AI to improve supplier communication
Build a chatbot for the procurement team
Cut the time to answer a supplier query from two days to two hours
Make the procurement process more modern
questions.why: A framed problem is one clear problem with a measurable goal.

questions.q: Your proof of concept is ready. Who should see the demo first?
options: The daily users who will actually work with it
The senior sponsor who approved the budget
The product team back at your company
Nobody, until it has no known failures
questions.why: Users find the failures that matter, so you show it to them before senior sponsors.

questions.q: An engagement ends with a working system and good evaluation results, but no one on the client side owns it. What is the likely outcome?
options: It keeps running fine because the results were good
The product team takes it over automatically
It usually fades away within months
The model improves on its own over time
questions.why: A good engagement needs a system, evidence, an owner and documents; if one is missing the work usually fades.

questions.q: A client lead asks a question you cannot answer yet. What response does the lesson favour?
options: Give your best confident guess so you look prepared
Change the subject to what you do know
Say you do not know yet and when you will find out
Ask them to send the question by email and forget it
questions.why: Saying you do not know yet and giving a date builds more trust than a confident guess.

questions.q: Which two questions does the lesson suggest for telling the four roles apart?
options: How senior are they, and how much do they charge?
What do they deliver, and who do they serve?
Which tools do they use, and which language do they code in?
How long have they worked there, and who is their manager?
questions.why: Asking what each role delivers and who it serves separates consultant, solutions engineer, product engineer and FDE.

questions.q: In your first week a client manager asks you for a strategy deck. What is the FDE response from the lesson?
options: Offer a one-page written recommendation plus a working build
Write the full deck, since that is what they asked for
Refuse and tell them FDEs do not write documents
Pass the request to the sales team
questions.why: The lesson suggests a short written recommendation plus a working build, so the output stays a working system.

questions.q: A client asks you to promise a new feature for all customers of your product. What should you do?
options: Promise it to keep the client happy
Build it as a general product feature right away
Ignore it, as it is outside your role
Log it for the product team and solve their case first
questions.why: The FDE logs repeat requests for product and focuses on solving this client's problem first.

questions.q: Which trap belongs to the solutions engineer role, and must be avoided by an FDE?
options: Stopping at the recommendation
Showing the happy path and hiding the hard cases
Building a general feature before understanding the client
Spending too long in discovery interviews
questions.why: The solutions engineer trap is showing only the happy path; an FDE shows failures too.

questions.q: During an engagement you keep a running log with three headings for the product team. Which headings does the lesson name?
options: Wins, losses, next steps
Bugs, features, questions
Built custom, asked for again, broke more than once
Data, integration, validation
questions.why: These three headings capture what should feed back to product from the client work.

questions.q: A pilot chatbot worked in the demo, but six months later nobody uses it. Where should you look first?
options: Swap in a bigger model
Rewrite the prompts from scratch
Add more features to make it attractive
Check the five gaps around the model: data, integration, validation, ownership, adoption
questions.why: The model is rarely the main problem; projects stall because of the five gaps around it.

questions.q: Support agents spend all day in an existing ticket tool. Where should your AI draft replies appear?
options: Inside the existing ticket tool
On a new standalone website
In a weekly email report
In a separate mobile app
questions.why: To close the integration gap you put output where people already work.

questions.q: When should you start building the test set of real cases with known correct answers?
options: After the demo, if the sponsor asks for numbers
In the first week
Only once the system is in production
Never, user feedback is enough
questions.why: The lesson says build the test set early, from real cases, instead of at the end.

questions.q: A sponsor says the owner of the new system will be 'the business'. Why is that a problem?
options: The business never pays for AI projects
Owners must always be engineers
Ownership only matters after go live
It is not a named person, so nobody is really responsible when it breaks
questions.why: 'The business' is not an owner; a named person who runs, fixes and decides on changes is.

questions.q: Why are LLM demos especially misleading?
options: Demos always use a weaker model than production
The presenter picks the inputs and retries until it looks right, unlike real messy use
Demos cannot show the model's output
Users are not allowed to watch demos
questions.why: In a demo you choose clean inputs and can retry, while real use is messy and nobody retries.

questions.q: You are learning SQL with an LLM. Following the program rule, what do you do first?
options: Write your own query or answer, then ask the model to find the gaps
Ask the model for the full solution and study it
Copy the model's explanation into your notes
Ask the model to write a summary for your journal
questions.why: The rule is that the AI may explain and check, but you must produce first.

questions.q: Which is the stronger learning prompt?
options: Write a SQL query that finds late orders.
Explain gross margin.
Here is my query and the error I get. Give me a hint about what is wrong, not the fixed query.
Summarise this chapter for me.
questions.why: A strong prompt works with what you already tried and leaves the thinking to you.

questions.q: The model gave a clear explanation of a rule you will act on tomorrow. What should you do?
options: Trust it, since it is well written
Ask the same model again until the answer looks the same
Skip checking because models are rarely wrong on rules
Verify the key fact against an official source
questions.why: Fluent text feels true, so you verify anything you will act on against an official source.

questions.q: You need to know how a client's company handles small invoice differences. Who is the best source?
options: An LLM, since it has read about accounting
Your pair partner or the people at that company
A general accounting textbook
A blog post on invoice matching
questions.why: Company-specific rules like a tolerance rule are set by each company, so a model cannot know them; ask the people.

questions.q: In your pair, the software person has typed for the whole session. What is wrong and what fixes it?
options: Nothing, the faster typist should drive
The domain person should leave and study alone
The pair is not working; swap driver and navigator on a timer
The navigator should take over the keyboard when they disagree
questions.why: If one person always drives the pair is not working, so swap roles every 25 to 30 minutes.
